patient.chief_complaint: High fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness developing over the past 48 hours in a 74-year-old man recently started on corticosteroids.
patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old man with a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, and monoclonal IgA gammopathy of undetermined significance presents to the emergency department with acute onset of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. For the preceding three months prior to this presentation, he had experienced fluctuating headaches, fatigue, proximal muscle weakness in his upper extremities, low-grade fevers up to 38.3 degrees Celsius, unintentional weight loss of approximately 7 kilograms, and diffuse joint pain with temporal tenderness. He was evaluated extensively as an outpatient including inflammatory markers, serum protein electrophoresis, blood cultures, echocardiography, and cross-sectional imaging of the chest and abdomen, which were largely unremarkable aside from an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and the known IgA monoclonal gammopathy. A presumptive diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica was made, and he was started on prednisolone 30 mg daily approximately two weeks ago, with initial improvement in his musculoskeletal symptoms. Ten days after starting prednisolone, he developed rapid-onset exertional exhaustion and returned to his primary care physician, who noted persistent low-grade fevers and referred him to the emergency department. Over the subsequent 48 hours, his condition deteriorated markedly with the development of high spiking fevers to 39 degrees Celsius, a progressively worsening generalized headache described as the worst of his life, photophobia, nausea with two episodes of vomiting, and pronounced neck stiffness. On arrival to the emergency department, he is febrile, tachycardic, and appears acutely toxic. He is alert but confused regarding the date. His neck is markedly rigid with positive meningeal signs. There is no rash.

results.title: Adjunctive Dexamethasone in Bacterial Meningitis
results.authors: de Gans J, van de Beek D
results.summary: Landmark RCT demonstrating that adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h x4 days) given before or with the first dose of antibiotics reduces unfavorable outcomes and mortality in adults with pneumococcal meningitis.

results.title: Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis - IDSA 2004
results.summary: IDSA guidelines recommend empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin + ampicillin (if Listeria risk) for adults >50 years. Adjunctive dexamethasone recommended for suspected pneumococcal meningitis. Duration of therapy for pneumococcal meningitis: 10-14 days.

results.title: Bacterial Meningitis in Immunocompromised Patients
results.summary: Immunocompromised patients (including those on corticosteroids) are at increased risk for bacterial meningitis and atypical organisms including Listeria. Higher mortality in this population. Empiric coverage must include ampicillin for Listeria in addition to standard ceftriaxone + vancomycin.

output.summary: Immunocompromised patients on corticosteroids are at elevated risk for bacterial meningitis and atypical pathogens including Listeria monocytogenes, with higher associated mortality. Adjunctive dexamethasone has established mortality benefit in pneumococcal meningitis in RCT data. Published guidelines recommend coverage for Listeria as part of empiric regimens in higher-risk populations.

output.proposed: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h + Vancomycin 1g IV q12h + Dexamethasone 10mg IV q6h
interactions: Ceftriaxone may cause false-positive urine glucose tests in patients on glucose monitoring
Vancomycin and ceftriaxone: no significant pharmacokinetic interaction, but combination increases nephrotoxicity risk - monitor renal function
warnings: Patient is already on prednisolone 30 mg daily - consider transitioning to dexamethasone for adjunctive meningitis treatment and discontinuing prednisolone to avoid excessive immunosuppression
Monitor renal function closely with vancomycin dosing - obtain vancomycin trough levels
Aspirin continuation: assess bleeding risk given potential coagulopathy in sepsis
alternatives: If penicillin-susceptible pneumococcus confirmed: may narrow to ceftriaxone monotherapy or high-dose IV penicillin G
Meropenem as alternative if cephalosporin allergy

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

differential.key_features: Lymphocyte-predominant CSF, normal-to-mildly elevated glucose, lower protein, lower CRP/procalcitonin — clinically distinguished by less toxic appearance
Temporal lobe MRI changes, seizures or focal deficits, lymphocytic CSF; HSV PCR required to exclude
Subacute onset, lymphocytic CSF, basilar enhancement, very low glucose — different tempo and pattern from this case
Typically in severely immunocompromised host; cryptococcal antigen and India ink exclude
Sudden thunderclap headache, xanthochromic CSF, hemorrhage on CT — none of these features present

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC with differential, CRP (or procalcitonin), paired blood glucose, coagulation, renal/liver function and HIV testing; results must not delay LP or empirical therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Inflammation/sepsis and LP safety context; blood values neither confirm nor exclude bacterial meningitis

optimal_actions.action: Draw blood cultures with susceptibility testing as early as possible, preferably before antimicrobials, but start empirical therapy immediately if LP/imaging is delayed
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pathogen and susceptibility, with collection timing recorded

optimal_actions.action: Perform LP with opening pressure, appearance, total/differential WBC, RBC, protein, CSF-to-blood glucose ratio, Gram stain, culture/susceptibility and relevant PCR; record whether collected before antibiotics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bacterial pattern and organism/susceptibility; PCR and culture yield depend on whether antibiotics preceded sampling

optimal_actions.action: Obtain non-contrast CT head to exclude mass effect, midline shift, basal cistern obliteration, or hydrocephalus that would contraindicate lumbar puncture in this patient with altered mental status and/or immunocompromise.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Absence of mass lesion, midline shift, or signs of impending herniation — confirms LP is safe.

optimal_actions.action: Verify compatibility of empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin if Listeria coverage indicated) and adjunctive dexamethasone with the patient's current medications, and confirm timing of dexamethasone BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No prohibitive interactions; confirmation of standard guideline-directed empiric regimen with dose adjustments as required.

optimal_actions.action: Search the literature for current guideline-directed empiric antibiotic selection by age and host factors and for the evidence base supporting adjunctive dexamethasone in pneumococcal meningitis.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Retrieval of IDSA 2004, ESCMID 2016, and De Gans 2002 to support empiric regimen and steroid timing.

useless_tools.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Per IDSA 2004, non-contrast CT head must precede lumbar puncture whenever any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal neurological deficit, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60). LP performed in undetected mass effect can precipitate fatal herniation.

critical_actions: Administer the first dose of empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion; do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or imaging beyond what is strictly needed for safety.
Give adjunctive dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue q6h for 4 days in confirmed pneumococcal meningitis.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.
Obtain CT head before LP because imaging-first criteria are present (altered mental status, immunocompromise, focal signs, papilledema, or age >60).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.
Reassess and de-escalate antibiotics based on Gram stain, culture, and susceptibility results.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
key_reasoning_points: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotic timing matters: every hour of delay after the first hour increases mortality. Antibiotics MUST precede imaging or LP if either would delay treatment >60 minutes.
CT before LP is mandated when any imaging-first criterion is present (altered mental status, focal signs, papilledema, recent seizure, immunocompromise, or age >60).
Adjunctive dexamethasone (10 mg IV q6h × 4 days) given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and unfavourable outcomes in pneumococcal meningitis (De Gans 2002, NEJM).
A negative CSF Gram stain (sensitivity ~60-90%, lower if antibiotic pretreated) does not exclude bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR or antigen testing retains sensitivity.
CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4 is more reliable than absolute CSF glucose for distinguishing bacterial from viral meningitis.
Empiric coverage must include vancomycin + ceftriaxone in adults; add ampicillin for Listeria coverage if age >50 or immunocompromised.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.
